intro: In Jenkinsburg, opossum work is almost always about the outbuildings. This very small community in northern Butts County is built on rural-acreage lots — houses paired with barns, sheds, and equipment buildings — and that gives the Virginia opossum exactly the ground-level shelter it favors. Heard hissing under the floor, found droppings in the garage, or watched one shuffle across the yard at night? Not every one needs removing: a yard visitor is a short-term guest, while an animal denned under a structure is the one to exclude.
extendedBody:
A Multi-Structure Setting Opossums Love

What defines Jenkinsburg for wildlife is its layout: small in population, large in lot size, with most properties carrying more than one building. The Virginia opossum is a nomadic opportunist that does not dig its own den — it occupies whatever sheltered, at-grade space is already open — so on a typical Jenkinsburg lot the candidates aren't just the crawlspace, but the barn, the shed, the equipment building, and the void under a deck or porch. The pine-hardwood remnants and farmed acreage around town keep a healthy opossum population on hand to fill those spaces, and because one animal succeeds another, an unsealed opening stays in use indefinitely.

When the Calls Come

Opossums breed across most of the year in central Georgia, so they appear in every season. The clear surge is in summer, when juveniles from that year's litters disperse on their own and wander into garages, sheds, and under-deck spaces — which is when many Jenkinsburg calls land.

Don't Remove the Ones Earning Their Keep

Plenty of Jenkinsburg opossum sightings are of an animal that is genuinely useful and simply moving through:

  • A low body temperature makes opossums very unlikely to carry rabies.
  • They eat large numbers of ticks — worth a lot on rural, wooded lots.
  • They hunt mice, rats, and insects, trimming the rodent base that attracts snakes.

A yard opossum with no structural den typically moves on within two to four weeks. Save the intervention for the animal that has taken up residence under the house, under a deck, or in one of the outbuildings, where the droppings and odor accumulate and a mother may be raising young.

Exclusion on a Working Rural Lot

Since opossums exploit existing gaps, prevention is about closing them — and on a Jenkinsburg property that is a whole-lot job, not just a house job:

  • Seal the house — crawlspace vents and deck and porch skirting — with 1/4-inch hardware cloth, trenched in and bent outward so true diggers can't tunnel under.
  • Seal the outbuildings the same way. Barns, sheds, and equipment buildings are the dens that get overlooked; address every structure an animal can get beneath.
  • Take away the easy meals — secured trash, no overnight pet food, and cleaned-up fruit and birdseed.
  • Verify the space is empty — including any pouch young — before the final sealing, so nothing is trapped inside. All trapping and removal follow Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division practice.

faqs.q: How much does opossum removal cost in Jenkinsburg, GA?
faqs.a: The exclusion drives the price more than the trapping. Pulling one opossum from a single crawlspace is at the low end; a Jenkinsburg rural lot where the house plus a barn or shed all need their ground-level gaps sealed costs more because there is more to close. An on-site look produces a firm estimate.

Largely no. They very rarely carry rabies, and their open-mouth hiss is a bluff rather than aggression. The concern with one denned under a structure or outbuilding is sanitation — droppings, odor, and fouled insulation — not danger, so those animals are removed and the access is closed.

faqs.q: Why do opossums keep getting under my Jenkinsburg buildings?
faqs.a: Because the lots here are rural and multi-structure, and opossums use any open, sheltered space at ground level — a crawlspace, an under-deck void, or a barn, shed, or equipment building. They don't dig their own way in; they reuse existing gaps, and a new animal takes over a vacated den until the opening is sealed.

faqs.q: Should I just let the opossum in my yard be?
faqs.a: If it has no den under a structure, yes — a yard-only opossum usually moves on within a few weeks and is doing useful work on ticks and rodents in the meantime. Act on the one that has settled under the house or an outbuilding.

faqs.q: When are opossums most active around Jenkinsburg?
faqs.a: Year-round, because of the long central-Georgia breeding season. The most noticeable period is summer, when juveniles disperse on their own and turn up in garages, sheds, and under decks across the area's rural lots.
